extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, publishers, researchers and practitioners interested in open peer review and open science
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and review comments for a systematic/PRISMA-style paper that aims to define 'open peer review' by collecting and analysing definitions and traits; covers methodological transparency, precise terminology, taxonomy of OPR traits, and mapping traits to problems and benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: PRISMA — describe information sources
rubrics_metrics.description: "7. - Describe all information sources (e.g., databases with dates of coverage, contact with study authors to identify additional studies) in the search and date last searched"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claiming a systematic review, explicitly list all information sources (databases, web searches, grey literature, date ranges) and provide the last-search date so the search universe is transparent and reproducible.

rubrics_metrics.name: PRISMA — present full electronic search strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: "8. Present full electronic search strategy for at least one database, including any limits used, such that it could be repeated."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide at least one complete database search string (with limits/filters) so other researchers can exactly reproduce the search; include how additional sources were identified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity about universe of literature and assessment details
rubrics_metrics.description: "There is a lack of clarity about the universe of literature that is being assessed, and of details about how it was assessed."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about inclusion/exclusion criteria, databases and other sources searched, supplementary methods (citation chasing, Google/Google Scholar, blogs, books), and how source selection/enrichment was performed to avoid appearing non-systematic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define listed types/traits when introduced
rubrics_metrics.description: "p7 – it is not helpful to list the seven types of openness without definitions."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When enumerating types or traits (e.g., seven types of openness), provide at least brief definitions immediately or signpost definitions to reduce reader confusion; avoid leaving key terms undefined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider and account for variants such as real-time open review
rubrics_metrics.description: "In my view the author does not pay enough attention to one important variant of open review, namely real-time review in the open... the ‘real-time’ variant occurs far more often, and ought to be included as one of the key traits within the umbrella definition."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly consider variants such as real-time community commenting and other emergent practices when defining the umbrella term; state whether such variants are core traits or dependent on other traits (and justify that position).

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate editorial selection from technical peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: "Throughout the article he appears to conflate editorial selection (whether a journal accepts a manuscript) with technical review (whether the work is sound and properly reported)."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide conceptual clarity by separating processes (editorial selection, technical review, publication cycles) and ensure claims about 'peer review problems' are tied to the correct process to avoid muddled arguments or unsupported inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish open reports from open identities
rubrics_metrics.description: "some journals use open reports without open identities – i.e. posting reports with published articles but without identifying the reviewer... The author writes as if open reports must always have open identities."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When discussing 'open reports' versus 'open identities', clarify that reports can be published without revealing reviewer names; explicitly state which combinations exist and give examples (e.g., EMBO).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use precise, unambiguous terminology (e.g., pre-review manuscripts vs preprints)
rubrics_metrics.description: "I think ‘open pre-review manuscripts’ is the wrong name for what the author is describing... he might like to consider the suggestions by Neylon et al. about this issue of terminology"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose clear, consistent terms and define them (e.g., distinguish 'open posting before formal review' (preprints) from 'posting authors’ version alongside peer review history'); avoid ambiguous phrasing like 'posting' that could be misread.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support claims of influence or impact with evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: "p10 – I wonder if the author has any evidence that PubPeer has been ‘a major influence’?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overstating the influence of platforms or practices without supporting evidence; either provide citations/data to back claims or moderate language (e.g., 'an important platform').

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid oversimplified causal claims (e.g., reasons for retraction)
rubrics_metrics.description: "This conflation is made worse when, for example, it is implied that the only reason for retraction is error."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful with causal attributions (e.g., retraction causes); acknowledge multiple causes and ensure assertions are supported by evidence or accompanied by nuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assert a 'unified definition' without justification
rubrics_metrics.description: "p11 – Conclusion. I don’t believe the author presents a unified definition of open peer review..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the literature or definitions are heterogeneous, avoid claiming a single unified definition; instead present an umbrella of traits and discuss contested elements and boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge benefits specific to contexts (e.g., open identity in medicine and COI scrutiny)
rubrics_metrics.description: "proponents of open identity review in medicine would also point out that it makes conflicts of interest much more apparent and subject to scrutiny."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing traits like open identity, discuss context-dependent benefits and harms (e.g., transparency of conflicts of interest in clinical fields) and cite stakeholders or evidence supporting these claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Map each OPR trait to the problems it aims to address and to Open Science goals
rubrics_metrics.description: "Two new sections have been added... which make clearer (1) the particular problems with traditional peer review that each OPR trait aims to address, and (2) how each trait can be related to the broader agenda of Open Science."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For each trait in the taxonomy, explicitly explain (a) which traditional peer review problem(s) it addresses, and (b) how it connects to Open Science principles, including examples or mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure references support claims and evidence is correctly interpreted
rubrics_metrics.description: "the references and evidence do not all support the broad claims made about ‘peer review’..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify that cited literature actually supports the assertions made; avoid broad claims that outstrip the evidence cited, and correct or soften claims where the citation does not fully back them.
